title: Little Words
description: I, you, he and she, this and that, the question words, and ada. Tiny words that hold every sentence together.

items.registerNotes: The safe, polite 'I' for strangers, shops, elders and work. After a noun it means my: rumah saya, my house.
With friends, a partner, family of your own age, and children. With anyone you don't know or who is older, say saya.
items.pitfallNote: Aku goes with kamu. With someone you'd call Bapak or Ibu, stick to saya.

items.registerNotes: For friends, people your age or younger, and children. To an older person or a stranger it's too familiar: use their name, or Bapak or Ibu, instead.
Polite but impersonal: you'll see it on signs, forms and ads, always with a capital A. Face to face, people say Bapak, Ibu or the person's name instead: Ibu mau ke mana? rather than Anda mau ke mana?

items.pitfallNote: One word for both, so dia alone doesn't say whether it's a man or a woman. It's for people, not things.
Kami leaves out the person you're talking to; kita includes them. To your host: Kami dari Selandia Baru (We're from New Zealand), because your host isn't one of 'us'.

items.registerNotes: Includes the person you're talking to: Kita makan di mana? (Where shall we eat?). In casual speech, especially in Jakarta, many people use kita for kami too.
For people, not things. After a noun it means their: rumah mereka, their house.

items.pitfallNote: Where it goes matters. Before a noun it makes a sentence: Ini kopi (This is coffee). After a noun it points: kopi ini (this coffee).

items.registerNotes: Itu rumah saya is 'That's my house', but rumah itu is 'that house'. After a noun it often just means 'the', for something you both know about.
It can stay where the answer would go: Mau apa? (What do you want?). Apa kabar? (How are you?) literally asks 'What news?'
Also the word for asking a name: Namanya siapa? (What's your name?). Ini punya siapa? asks 'Whose is this?'

items.pitfallNote: Di mana asks where something is. For where to, it's ke mana (Mau ke mana?), and for where from, dari mana (Dari mana?). Always two words.
Only for questions: Kapan pulang? (When are you going home?). For 'when' in a statement, use waktu or kalau.

items.english: how much, how many; what number
items.registerNotes: Berapa harganya? (How much is it?), Berapa orang? (How many people?), Jam berapa? (What time is it?), Umurnya berapa? (How old are you?)
Mengapa is the formal, written word. Kenapa? on its own also means 'What's the matter?'
In casual speech it shortens to gimana. Bagaimana kalau …? makes a suggestion: Bagaimana kalau besok? (How about tomorrow?)

items.english: there is, there are; to be (somewhere)
items.registerNotes: Ada air? asks 'Is there any water?' or 'Do you have water?'. Pak Budi ada? asks whether Mr Budi is in. Tidak ada is 'there isn't any' or 'not here'.
items.pitfallNote: It isn't 'is' before a describing word: Saya capek (I'm tired), not Saya ada capek.
